summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol, a reliable transport protocol originally designed to carry telephone signaling over IP but usable more broadly. The objects let managers monitor associations and statistics.

eli5.summary: SCTP is a way of delivering messages reliably. This document defines a standard report so a manager can see how well it is working.

questions: how to monitor sctp with snmp
how to abort an sctp association with snmp
subtitle: The standard set of SNMP objects for watching an SCTP implementation: counters, settings and per-association details.

tldr.problem: Operators need a common way to monitor SCTP, a reliable transport protocol built to carry telephone signaling over IP, without a different tool for every vendor.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3873 defines an SNMP MIB module under mib-2 {1 3 6 1 2 1} 104 with layer-wide statistics and parameters, a table of associations with address sub-tables, and optional reverse lookup tables.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read how many associations exist, how they started and ended, what timers are configured, and the state and addresses of each association. Only one object, the association state, can be written.

today: RFC 3873 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the MIB module for the SCTP protocol specified in RFC 2960.

sections.title: What the SCTP MIB Is For
sections.content:
The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a reliable transport protocol that runs on top of a connectionless packet network such as IP. It was designed to carry public switched telephone network (PSTN) signaling messages, but the RFC says it is capable of broader applications. The protocol itself is defined in RFC 2960.

RFC 3873 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module, which describes the minimum set of objects needed to manage an SCTP implementation. The objects are based on the TCP MIB work (an update of RFC 2012) and on the address types of RFC 3291.
sections.eli5: A MIB is a list of questions you are allowed to ask a machine, such as how many connections are open. This one lists the questions for SCTP.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
The module is a standard SMIv2 module (STD 58, RFCs 2578, 2579 and 2580) whose objects are normally read through SNMP. It sits at sctpMIB, number 104 under mib-2 {1 3 6 1 2 1}, and has two branches: sctpObjects and sctpMibConformance.

Under sctpObjects are two groups of scalars, sctpStats and sctpParameters, followed by tables: sctpAssocTable, sctpAssocLocalAddrTable, sctpAssocRemAddrTable and five reverse lookup tables.

No row in any table can be created through SNMP. Rows cannot be deleted either, with one exception described below for the association table.
sections.eli5: It is like a filing cabinet with a few drawers for totals and settings and a few drawers with one folder per connection. You can look in the drawers, but you cannot add folders yourself.

sections.title: Statistics and Parameters
sections.content:
The statistics use Counter32 and Gauge32, plus Counter64 for counters likely to wrap around in less than one hour. The state-related ones are modeled on the TCP MIB but adapted to SCTP states: sctpCurrEstab counts associations that are ESTABLISHED, SHUTDOWN-RECEIVED or SHUTDOWN-PENDING, and sctpActiveEstabs and sctpPassiveEstabs count associations that were started by the local or the remote side. sctpAborteds counts ungraceful endings and sctpShutdowns counts graceful ones. Others cover out of the blue packets, checksum errors, chunks and packets sent and received, and fragmented and reassembled user messages.

The parameters are read-only values for the whole SCTP layer. The retransmission timeout algorithm is other or vanj (Van Jacobson's algorithm, the default), because SCTP defines vanj as the one to use. Default values are listed alongside.
sections.eli5: The statistics are like a scoreboard that counts how many calls were made, finished politely or hung up suddenly. The parameters are the rules of the game, such as how long to wait before trying again.

sections.title: The Association Tables
sections.content:
The main table, sctpAssocTable, holds information per association and is indexed by sctpAssocId. The MIB does not say what value to use, only that it must be unique within the table. Its columns include the remote host name, local and remote ports, the primary remote address, the heartbeat interval, the state, the number of inbound and outbound streams, and counters such as T1 and T2 timer expiries and retransmitted chunks.

Two more tables share the same index: sctpAssocLocalAddrTable lists the local IP addresses and sctpAssocRemAddrTable lists the remote addresses with per-address information. This reflects SCTP multihoming, where one association can use several addresses. A row in sctpAssocTable is created when the association is being set up, at the COOKIE-ECHO message (originating side) or the COOKIE-ACK message (server side). The remote host name is a zero-length string if the peer gave none.

Addresses use the InetAddressType and InetAddress types. Only IPv4 and IPv6 are required, and DNS names are never stored because they are resolved before connection setup.
sections.eli5: Each connection gets its own folder with its own number. Because an SCTP connection can use several addresses, there are extra sheets listing every address on each side.

sections.title: Reverse Lookups and Aborting
sections.content:
Five optional reverse lookup tables let a manager find associations without walking a large table. They can be searched by local port, remote port, remote host name, remote primary IP address or any remote IP address. Their rows appear and disappear on their own as the matching rows of sctpAssocTable do, and an operator cannot create or delete them.

The only way to delete rows is to write the value deleteTCB(9) to sctpAssocState, which aborts the association. The state object otherwise takes values such as closed(1), cookieWait(2), established(4) and shutdownSent(6).
sections.eli5: Reverse lookup is like an index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page, you look up a name and jump to the right place. The one thing you can do to a connection is tell the computer to hang up on it.

sections.title: Conformance and Compiling Notes
sections.content:
The conformance branch defines four groups: sctpLayerParamsGroup, sctpStatsGroup, sctpPerAssocParamsGroup and sctpInverseGroup. General layer and per-association parameters and statistics are mandatory, while all the inverse lookup tables are optional.

The RFC warns that compiling the module may produce warnings that some row indexes can exceed the OID size limit. This is because InetAddress and OCTET STRING indexes may be up to 255 octets, while SNMP allows at most 128 sub-identifiers. The RFC states that the limits will not be reached by any address type in current use.
sections.eli5: Some parts of the report are required and some are optional extras. A note also warns that very long names could be too big for the old tools to read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The one writable object, sctpAssocState, allows termination of an arbitrary connection, so unauthorized access could cause a denial of service. The readable objects are sensitive too: they reveal active associations, local and peer IP addresses, ports that are open and the processes involved, which an attacker could use to choose attacks without running a port scanner.

The RFC says SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. The objects also have privacy implications because they disclose who is connecting to what hosts.
sections.eli5: The report shows who is talking to whom, and one button can hang up a connection. So only trusted people should be allowed to see it or press the button.
